interview_context.setting_or_workflow_context: oncology clinical decision-making and research workflow with interest in literature-based questions, evidence summaries, and patient-specific management considerations

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I used Open Evidence a bit, which is pretty good. I think it's helpful for answering clinical questions... I usually also like to confirm with... colleagues... it can be helpful just to make sure we're on the right track.
segments.rationale: The participant describes Open Evidence as useful for answering questions and checking direction, but also says they confirm with colleagues and notes limitations in specialty-specific and institution-specific applicability.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: The thing I did find was helpful is if you were asking specifically, like, what does the literature say about this?... it tells you all the evidence... there's no evidence that this helps, these are all the studies.
segments.rationale: The participant explicitly says this style was helpful when the question was narrowly about what the literature says and valued the listing of studies and evidence.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I liked the blue one the best... it was very comprehensive... it actually stopped and was like, well, first, you should actually... check for other causes, too... and others didn't necessarily recommend that.
segments.rationale: The participant favors the report that broadened the workup and caught additional considerations other reports missed.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: It was nice that it kind of presented, like, these are the options... but some of them kind of provided, like, this is the recommendation that I would have for this patient... they haven't seen the patient.
segments.rationale: The participant likes option-framing but objects when the report makes a firm recommendation without enough patient-specific information or knowledge of patient goals.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: If you're gonna say there's no difference, that's an interpretation... it could be P equals .059 and a huge clinical benefit... presenting that data is very helpful... it assesses the quality of the evidence.
segments.rationale: The participant distinguishes between reporting the data and claiming there is no difference, and wants the underlying numbers and evidence quality rather than compressed conclusions.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I would err more on the side of less interpretation... I like having the facts presented and to make my own interpretation... if it's saying, like, this is my recommendation and this is why... that's concerning to me.
segments.rationale: The participant clearly states a preference for fact presentation over model-led recommendation and labels unsolicited interpretation as concerning.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I had... an R markdown... PDF, and I just said, turn this data into a results paragraph... I still went back and double-checked them. But it was right, and it did it very well.
segments.rationale: The participant reports a concrete non-clinical use case where the tool saved time and performed well, while still requiring verification.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: If I'm looking for an interpretation, that's fine, but I think sometimes they do it by default... it hasn't seen the patient... it hasn't asked the patient about... values and goals... there's certainly no physical exam.
segments.object_of_evaluation: trust, patient context, decision support scope
segments.rationale: The participant accepts interpretation only when explicitly requested and explains why default interpretation is risky in the absence of patient interaction and exam information.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Local control really matters for some patients... for their quality of life... I think there's just a lot of things where you could easily be like, there's no benefit to this. But maybe there is.
segments.rationale: The participant warns that a report can miss meaningful benefit when it compresses complex situations into a simple no-benefit conclusion.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I like the ones that have, like, a summary at the top... at least alongside some data... I definitely think having, like, a next steps or, like, follow-up questions thing is... important to have.
segments.rationale: The participant wants concise summaries, but only when supported by visible data, and explicitly asks for next steps and follow-up questions.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Having, like, the actual data... numbers in it... there was one where it had, like, a forest plot, and I thought that was nice... I thought the references overall were pretty good.
segments.rationale: The participant values concrete numbers, found at least one graph helpful, and reports that the references they checked appeared real and credible.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Maybe you can also choose... what do you want in interpretation... sometimes it is helpful... but... if it's written there, you're going to be more likely to believe it.
segments.rationale: The participant proposes adjustable interpretation depth and explains that written recommendations can unduly influence belief even when they are uncertain.

themes.theme_name: Useful for evidence retrieval, risky as default decision-maker
themes.theme_definition: The participant repeatedly describes AI reports as useful when they surface literature, organize evidence, and save time. The value drops when the system shifts from presenting evidence to making patient-specific recommendations without enough context. The participant draws a line between evidence support and decision authority.

representative_quotes.quote: What does the literature say about this?... it tells you all the evidence.
I would err more on the side of less interpretation.

themes.confidence_basis: Repeated across many segments with direct statements about both utility and concern.

themes.theme_name: Show the numbers, not just the conclusion
themes.theme_definition: The participant wants the report to display hard data, endpoint results, and evidence quality rather than collapsing findings into simplified verbal claims. Numeric results are treated as necessary for independent clinician judgment. Summaries are acceptable only when visibly tied to supporting data.

representative_quotes.quote: Presenting that data is very helpful.
Having... the actual data... numbers in it.

themes.confidence_basis: This preference is stated clearly in multiple segments and linked to several concrete examples.

themes.theme_name: Patient context changes what counts as the right answer
themes.theme_definition: The participant stresses that missing variables, patient goals, physical exam findings, and subtle clinical details can materially alter recommendations. Because those factors are often absent from prompts, the participant is wary of overly certain AI conclusions. Benefit depends on context, not just literature headlines.

representative_quotes.quote: It hasn't asked the patient about... values and goals.
There's no benefit to this. But maybe there is.

themes.confidence_basis: The concern appears repeatedly and is grounded in several distinct examples.

themes.theme_name: Best report style combines summary, evidence, and next steps
themes.theme_definition: The participant's preferred report is neither a bare literature dump nor a single top-line recommendation. It should combine a concise summary, visible supporting data, practical next steps, and prompts for missing information. The participant also sees some value in visuals and good references within that structure.

representative_quotes.quote: Having... a next steps or... follow-up questions thing is... important.
I liked the blue one the best... it was very comprehensive.

themes.confidence_basis: Supported by multiple segments, though some design choices remain explicitly unresolved by the participant.

analytic_memos.summary: The participant sees clear value in AI tools for literature retrieval, answering direct evidence questions, and saving time in research-related writing tasks. They are notably more comfortable with the model as an evidence organizer than as an autonomous interpreter or recommender. A recurring concern is that reports may sound authoritative while lacking critical patient-specific details such as goals, exam findings, or other omitted variables. The participant strongly prefers that the report expose the underlying numbers and evidence quality rather than replace them with compressed verbal claims. They also prefer reports that present options and reasoning over a single directive recommendation. Structurally, they want a summary tied closely to data, plus explicit next steps and prompts for missing information. Overall, their perspective is favorable toward AI-assisted evidence synthesis but cautious about default interpretation and clinical overreach.
tensions_or_tradeoffs: A concise summary is useful, but if placed too prominently it may discourage reading the supporting evidence.
Interpretation can be helpful when explicitly requested, but risky when delivered by default.
A direct answer to a narrow literature question can be valuable, but the same report style may be insufficient for broader management decisions.
Firm recommendations are efficient, but option-based framing better preserves clinician judgment under uncertainty.
open_questions_for_next_interview: When does a participant want a literature-first report versus a management-oriented report with next steps?
What exact numeric fields or endpoints are most important to surface across different oncology use cases?
How should a report visually separate raw evidence from interpretation so clinicians do not over-trust the latter?
What is the best way to prompt users for missing patient context before a report is finalized?
How much customization over interpretation depth would participants actually use in practice?
